text: Now let the numbers leave the line. A complex number is a point in the plane, or an arrow from zero to that point. Multiplying two of them multiplies their lengths and adds their angles. Multiplying by i keeps the length the same and turns the arrow a quarter turn. So what is i times i?

Two quarter turns make a half turn, so i times i is minus one. Lengths multiply and angles add, so a slide rule for complex numbers needs two rulers. One for length, which multiplies, so it uses the logarithm we just built. And one for angle, which simply adds.

The complex exponential packs both together. Feed it x plus i times y. The real part x sets the length, e to the x. The imaginary part y sets the angle. For instance, take x to be the logarithm of two, and y to be a half pi: the length is two, the angle a quarter turn, so we land on two i.

Watch what that does to a grid. On the left is the input plane. Each horizontal line keeps one angle, so it goes to a ray from zero. Each vertical line keeps one length, so it goes to a circle. But a vertical line is infinitely long, and a circle closes after one lap. So each vertical line wraps around its circle again and again.

Zero and two pi times i are different inputs, and both land on one. So do four pi times i and minus two pi times i. Climbing two pi up the input plane carries the output once around its circle, back to where it started.
Here is a question. Which inputs land on minus one?

Minus one has length one, so the real part of the input is the logarithm of one, which is zero. Its angle is a half turn, pi. But pi plus any whole number of laps points the same way. So the inputs are pi times i, three pi times i, minus pi times i, and so on: a whole column of them, two pi apart. Every one is a logarithm of minus one.

The same goes for every nonzero number. Its logarithms share one real part, the logarithm of its length, and have a whole column of angles, one for each lap. Only zero is left out. Its length would have to be e to some x, and that is never zero. In the complex numbers, the exponential is a dial that forgets laps, just like the folded slide rule.

If a number has a whole column of logarithms, can we at least choose one in a sensible, continuous way? Start at one, choose the logarithm zero, and walk the number slowly around the circle of radius one. Keep the logarithm moving smoothly along with it.

As the number turns, its logarithm climbs straight up, because only the angle changes. A quarter of the way round, the logarithm is pi over two times i. Halfway round, at minus one, it is pi times i. When the number arrives back at one, what is the logarithm?

Two pi times i. The number came back. The logarithm did not. It finished one lap higher in the column than where it began. Go around again and it climbs again. Go the other way and it comes back down.

A loop that does not go around zero behaves differently. Here is a circle off to one side, which zero is not inside. Walk the number once around it, carrying the logarithm along as before. Will the logarithm come back to where it began?
It does: it drifts up and down, and returns exactly. What matters is how many times the loop winds around zero. That count is the winding number, and every lap moves the logarithm by two pi times i.

Could some other choice of logarithm be continuous all the way round? Try the obvious candidate: the logarithm whose angle stays between minus pi and pi. Walk round again, comparing it with ours, and track the gap in whole laps. The gap sits at zero until the number passes minus one, then jumps down a lap, because the candidate's angle leaps from pi to minus pi. So that candidate breaks at minus one.

Now suppose someone hands us a logarithm that is continuous everywhere on the circle. At every point it differs from ours by a whole number of laps, because both undo the same exponential. A gap that is always a whole number of laps, and varies continuously, can never jump from one whole number to the next, so it stays fixed all the way round.

Now follow both back to one. Theirs is a function of the point, so it returns to exactly the value it started with. Ours finishes two pi times i higher. So the gap has changed by one lap, and we just saw that it cannot change. That is a contradiction. No continuous logarithm exists on any loop that winds around zero. Something has to give.

What gives is the freedom to walk all the way around. Draw a line from zero out to infinity, and forbid crossing it. Now no loop can go around zero, and a continuous choice becomes possible. The line is called a branch cut.

The usual choice removes zero and the negative numbers, and keeps angles strictly between minus pi and pi. The result is the principal logarithm, written with a capital L. On this cut plane it is a single, well behaved function, with derivative one over z at every point, just as on the positive numbers. For example, i has length one and a quarter turn of angle, so Log of i is pi over two times i, and Log of minus i is minus pi over two times i.

Here is where the cut plane goes. The principal logarithm unrolls it into a horizontal strip, between height minus pi and height pi. Circles become vertical segments. Rays become horizontal lines. Now roll it back, and mark the two sides of the cut: one just above it, one just below. Where will they end up on the strip?

They land on opposite edges of the strip, the top edge and the bottom edge. That is because just above the cut the angle is close to pi, and just below it, close to minus pi. So a path that crosses the cut would have to jump by two pi.

The cut is a choice, not a crack. Cut along the upward imaginary axis instead, and the angles run over a different window, from minus three halves of pi up to a half pi. Or cut along a spiral. Any curve that runs from zero out to infinity without crossing itself will do: in the plane that is left, no loop can wind around zero. Zero is the one point every cut must touch. It is called the branch point.

Two cautions. On the negative numbers themselves, the usual convention assigns the angle pi, so the principal value exists there too. But it jumps: just below the cut, the angles are close to minus pi. And the principal logarithm undoes the exponential from one side only. Exponentiating the logarithm of z gives back z for every nonzero z. But the logarithm of e to the w gives back w only when the height of w is above minus pi and at most pi. That is the strip, with its top edge added by the convention.

On the positive numbers, the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms. Does that survive the cut? Take a number of length one, at an angle of three quarters of pi. Square it. The lengths multiply to one, and the angles add to one and a half pi. But the principal logarithm only reports angles in its window, from minus pi up to pi. So what angle will it report for the square?

Not one and a half pi: that is outside the window. It reports the same direction as minus a half pi. So the sum of the two logarithms is one and a half pi times i, while the logarithm of the product is minus a half pi times i. They differ by two pi times i, exactly one lap.

This is the slide rule's decimal point again. When the sum of the angles runs past the window, the chosen logarithm drops a lap, just as the slide rule's reading dropped a factor of ten. The rule that survives is this: the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms, plus a whole number of laps. The rule did not break. It now keeps a lap count. For our square, the count is minus one: one lap down.

That lap count hides inside a famous puzzle. Minus one is i times i. Write i as the square root of minus one. Combine the two roots into the root of minus one times minus one. That is the root of one, which is one. So minus one equals one. Which step broke?

Combining the roots. Here a square root is e to the power of half a logarithm. Each minus one has principal angle pi, so the two roots together turn by pi and point at minus one. But the product, one, has principal angle zero, not two pi. Halving the lost lap leaves a half turn, and a half turn is a factor of minus one. The root of a product equals the product of the roots only up to that sign.
